To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the best predictor for AST performance is the ASR word error rate, and that differences between ASR and AST performance are correlated with how phonetic and lexical information are encoded in the later layers of the model.

the size of the ASR pretraining data and the word error rate (WER) of the pretrained ASER model are the two most important factors in determining AST performance; that pretraining and augmenting the data are complementary, and that pretraining on a language related to the AST source improves AST performance.

1) the word error rate on the ASR pretraining dataset is the best predictor of AST performance; 2) ASR pretraining is most effective when the source and target languages are related; 3) ASR pre training and data augmentation yield complimentary benefits for AST.

the following question: How can we leverage pre training on ASR data in order to improve AST for low resource languages?
the question of what factors affect the effectiveness of pretraining for AST and what factors affect how well pretraining and data augmentations can be combined.
the question of how to best combine pretraining, data augmentation, and multilingual models for low resource speech to text translation.

pretraining and augmentation can be combined effectively to improve AST performance for low resource languages.

pretraining on ASR data from a high-resource language can be an effective tool to improve the performance of low resource speech to text translation systems, especially when the pretraining data is of a good quality and the source and target languages are related.

for low resource speech to text translation, the most important factor for pretraining is the ASR performance of the pretrained model, and that pretraining can be combined with data augmentation to yield further benefits.
